new_statements.translation: Colorado stress follows general rules, and some words are distinguished only by stress. Note the following examples: dehuí 'brush', déhui 'a kind of fish', mérana'e 'is waiting', merána'e 'is listening'. But with few exceptions, stress falls on the last syllable of the root of a word. Then, when suffixes are added, the stress may move, passing to one of the suffixes or, rarely, to another syllable of the root. [...] But note how the stress moves when the suffixes 'ca' and ''e' are added, giving meracá'e 'listened'. And in the case of lápalo 'lizard', when the suffix 'chi' is added the result is lapalóchi 'of the lizard'.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Default: primary stress on the final syllable of the root (root-final stress), regardless of following suffixes; but stress is lexically/morphologically contrastive in some pairs (mérana'e vs merána'e, déhui vs dehuí) and certain suffixes (e.g. -ca 'past', -chi) attract or shift stress rightward off the root. Stressed syllables carry higher pitch.
new_statements.exceptions: 'Con pocas excepciones': minimal pairs distinguished only by stress (dehuí/déhui; mérana'e 'is waiting' vs merána'e 'is listening'); stress shifts onto some suffixes (meracá'e) or to another root syllable (lápalo -> lapalóchi). Moore 1966:96 adds that accent 'cambia muchas veces al agregar sufijos' and differs between dialects; Moore 1979 NF12 notes unstressed vowels devoice before the aspiration.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level 'acento prosódico' defined relative to the root; examples are citation forms and inflected verb words; intonation section notes pitch peaks align with the stressed syllable.
new_statements.identity_note: Moore's 1966-1979 SIL work describes 'Colorado' = Tsafiki (colo1256, ISO cof) of Santo Domingo de los Colorados; same language, older exonym. Moore 1966 notes accent differs 'de dialecto en dialecto' and that his accent marks reflect a single (unnamed) dialect in isolation forms.

sources.note: p.5: stress ('acento prosódico') follows general rules and some word pairs are distinguished only by stress (dehuí/déhui, mérana'e/merána'e); with few exceptions stress falls on the LAST SYLLABLE OF THE ROOT; when suffixes are added stress may move onto a suffix or, rarely, to another root syllable (merána'e 'is listening' vs meracá'e 'listened'; lápalo -> lapalóchi). Pitch is generally higher on stressed syllables.

sources.note: Phonological notes NF 1-14: NF 3 says the Colorado orthography writes the tilde only on confusable words (mérae 'espera' vs meraé 'escuchó') and the lessons use Spanish tilde norms; NF 12 unstressed vowels between a voiceless consonant and the aspiration devoice. No positional stress rule stated.

sources.note: p.96 §5: accent is one of two sounds normally not. marked only in a few words that could be confused, e.g. 'merano' oír vs 'mérano' esperar; the dictionary follows Spanish tilde rules; 'El acento cambia muchas veces al agregar sufijos, y también hay diferencias de acento de dialecto en dialecto'; accent given is of one dialect, word pronounced in isolation. No positional rule.
